newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trichet says French deficit can be reduced.
newsitem.headline: Trichet says French deficit can be reduced.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said on Friday he believed that the country's 1997 deficit could be reduced but it depended on decisions being taken.
"Clearly we can lower the deficit, it's a question of the decisions to be taken to bring it down," Trichet told Europe 1 radio.
Trichet would not be drawn on how low the deficit could be reduced but said it was "clear we must make sure the objective of our country for 1997 is the same as for the 13 other countries".
He said earlier that 14 out of 15 European Union members were aiming to reduce their public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, or less, in 1997.
He said that if France failed to match the performance of other countries it would be penalized by higher interest rates.
"We would lose if we don't go on that (deficit-cutting) route," he said. He said a lower deficit would lay the basis for higher growth and job creation.

The Socialist government has said it is determined to launch the single currency on time on January 1, 1999. But it has urged a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty goal of limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
He said he was convinced of the new Socialist-led government's "commitment to Europe" and was certain it would take the decisions necessary to respect that commitment.
He added that he believed France and Germany would be ready for the introduction of the euro along with a "large number of (other) countries".
He added that the franc, which has been under some pressure in recent days, was "very solid" and there was no "problem of any sort" with it.
Trichet said French economic fundamentals were good and showed a recovery in economic growth. "The French economy is going well. We have to consolidate confidence," he said.
He repeated that the French economy would probably be growing at a rate of three percent at the end of 1997.
